cards.explanation: The answer is False. Nadab, Jeroboam's son and king of Israel, does evil in the sight of the LORD. The text says he “…walked in the way of his father and in his sin, which he had caused Israel to commit.” (1 Kings 15:26) No break, no fresh start, just the same road with a new king on it.

The answer is Ahijah the Shilonite. He is the prophet the text names here, the one through whom the LORD spoke this word (1 Kings 15:29). When the LORD says something, friends, it lands right where He said it would.

The answer is that Jeroboam sinned and made Israel sin. The text says it was “…because of the sins Jeroboam had committed and had caused Israel to commit, and because he had provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger.” (1 Kings 15:30) Notice it isn't only his own sin, friends. It's also the sin he caused Israel to commit.

The answer is war. The text says, “…there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel throughout their days.” (1 Kings 15:32) Two kingdoms, two kings, and no handshake in sight. Remember, this is the split that began back in 1 Kings 12:19-20.

The answer is that He raised him from nothing to be ruler. God says, “…I lifted you out of the dust and made you ruler over My people Israel…” (1 Kings 16:2) Dust is about as low as it gets, and God raised Baasha from there to the throne. That's what makes the rest of the verse so sharp, friends.

The answer is Jeroboam. God says, “…I will make your house like that of Jeroboam son of Nebat…” (1 Kings 16:3) Baasha wiped out Jeroboam's house, and now his own gets the same ending. The path he copied leads to the same place, friends.

The answers are Tirzah and Elah. Baasha was buried in Tirzah, the same city where he reigned (1 Kings 15:33, 16:6). That's where the throne sat during his twenty-four years. His son Elah reigned in his place (1 Kings 16:6), so Elah is the next king in the line. Remember that name, friends.

The answer is True. The text says the word came “…because of all the evil he had done in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger with the work of his hands and becoming like the house of Jeroboam, and also because Baasha had struck down the house of Jeroboam.” (1 Kings 16:7) So striking down Jeroboam's house is one of the reasons listed. It's right there in the sum-up, friends.

The answer is Zimri, commander of half his chariots. He was Elah's servant, and the text says he conspired against Elah while Elah was in Tirzah getting drunk at Arza's house (1 Kings 16:9). Then Zimri struck Elah down and reigned in his place (1 Kings 16:10).

The answer is Jehu. Jehu the prophet, the son of Hanani, is the one the LORD spoke through against Baasha (1 Kings 16:1, 12). It's a word the LORD had spoken, friends, and now it comes true. Zimri carries it out.

The answer is False. The text says it was “…because of all the sins Baasha and his son Elah had committed and had caused Israel to commit, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols.” (1 Kings 16:13) Both father and son are named. Elah wasn't just standing by.
The answer is seven. The text says Zimri “…reigned in Tirzah for seven days.” (1 Kings 16:15) A week is all he gets, friends. That's a shorter run than most of my cookie batches.

The answer is that they proclaim Omri, the army commander, king. The people in the camp heard that Zimri had conspired against the king and struck him down. Then “…there in the camp that very day, all Israel proclaimed Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel.” (1 Kings 16:16) The troops act that same day, friends. They make their own commander the king.

The answer is True. The text says Zimri died “…because of the sins he had committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD and following the example of Jeroboam and the sin he had committed and had caused Israel to commit.” (1 Kings 16:19) Jeroboam's example shows up again, friends. It keeps showing up in this passage.

The answer is that Omri's side wins and he becomes king. The text says, “…the followers of Omri proved stronger than those of Tibni son of Ginath. So Tibni died and Omri became king.” (1 Kings 16:22) Half the people backed each man, and Omri's side came out stronger. Then Omri takes the throne.

The answer is Samaria. Omri bought the hill from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city there, “…calling it Samaria after the name of Shemer, who had owned the hill.” (1 Kings 16:24) The city is named for the man who owned the hill. Samaria will matter for the rest of this passage, friends.

The answer is False. The text says, “…Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD and acted more wickedly than all who were before him.” (1 Kings 16:25) The next verse says he walked in all the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in his sins (1 Kings 16:26). The city is new, friends, but the way he walks isn't.

The answer is that he does more evil than all of them. The text says, “…Ahab son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him.” (1 Kings 16:30) That includes his own father, who had already acted more wickedly than those before him (1 Kings 16:25). The bar keeps going up, friends, and so does the evil.

The answer is Baal. The text says Ahab “…proceeded to serve and worship Baal.” (1 Kings 16:31) Baal is a false god. The next verse says Ahab set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he had built.

The answer is temple. The text says, “…Ahab set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he had built in Samaria.” (1 Kings 16:32) Ahab didn't just join in, friends. He had built a temple for Baal, and it was in Samaria.

The answer is an Asherah pole. The text says, “Then he set up an Asherah pole.” (1 Kings 16:33) First the altar for Baal, then the Asherah pole. The text says that is how Ahab did more to provoke the LORD than all the kings of Israel before him.

The answer is his firstborn son and his youngest son, and I think this one hurts, friends. The text says, “At the cost of Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and at the cost of Segub his youngest he set up its gates…” (1 Kings 16:34) The cost was his sons. It's a heavy verse, and I won't make light of it.

The answer is True. The text says it happened “…according to the word that the LORD had spoken through Joshua son of Nun.” (1 Kings 16:34) Joshua, Israel's leader after Moses, spoke that word about Jericho long before, when he said whoever rebuilds the city will do it at the cost of his firstborn and his youngest (Joshua 6:26). It's a hard verse, friends, but the text ties it to that word.
